scenario.title: The Second Round - Watergate Part 1

pressureEvents: Wills completes his second round and finds the garage latch taped again — the call to the Second District becomes unavoidable.
McCord's walkie-talkie, volume turned low, fails to carry Baldwin's belated warning before the stairwell door opens.
Officers Shoffler, Barrett, and Leeper reach the sixth-floor landing and begin working the corridor toward Suite 600.

open_threads.source: Frank Wills, Security Officer's Log, Watergate Office Building, June 17, 1972, National Archives, NAID 304970
open_threads.historical_record: Frank Wills's Security Officer's Log for June 17, 1972 (National Archives, NAID 304970) records the discovery of tape on the garage-level stairwell door latch bolts and the call to the Second District. The log records the second discovery and the police call in a single block entered at 1:47 AM; it does not subdivide the interval or separately record the moment Wills completed his earlier round and first encountered and removed the tape, so the precise timing of the first discovery and removal is not recoverable from this document.

open_threads.source: Alfred Baldwin testimony, Senate Select Committee on Presidential Campaign Activities; Los Angeles Times interview with Baldwin, October 5, 1972
open_threads.historical_record: Alfred Baldwin's testimony before the Senate Select Committee on Presidential Campaign Activities and his October 5, 1972 Los Angeles Times interview establish that he was stationed in Room 723 of the Howard Johnson Motor Lodge and was serving as lookout and radio monitor. These sources record that Baldwin transmitted a warning to the entry team. They do not record the specific visual details Baldwin observed — what he saw, in what sequence, and what assessment he formed — before transmitting; the content of his observation at that moment is not recoverable from these sources.

open_threads.source: Alfred Baldwin testimony, Senate Select Committee on Presidential Campaign Activities; Los Angeles Times interview with Baldwin, October 5, 1972
open_threads.historical_record: Alfred Baldwin's testimony before the Senate Select Committee on Presidential Campaign Activities and his Los Angeles Times interview of October 5, 1972 establish that he transmitted a warning and that the warning was received too late to allow the entry team to evade arrest. These sources record the outcome — the team did not escape — but do not establish the precise content of the transmission, the exact moment it was sent relative to the officers' entry into the building, or the specific volume setting of McCord's walkie-talkie at the moment of receipt.

choice_echoes.source: Frank Wills, Security Officer's Log, Watergate Office Building, June 17, 1972, National Archives, NAID 304970; Washington Metropolitan Police Department arrest report, June 17, 1972
choice_echoes.historical_record: Frank Wills discovered tape on the garage-level stairwell door latch bolts for the second time at approximately 1:47 AM on June 17, 1972. He had removed tape from the same doors during an earlier round on the same night. The Security Officer's Log and the Metropolitan Police Department arrest report both record the second discovery as the event that prompted his call to the Second District.

choice_echoes.source: Frank Wills, Security Officer's Log, Watergate Office Building, June 17, 1972, National Archives, NAID 304970; Washington Metropolitan Police Department arrest report, June 17, 1972
choice_echoes.historical_record: Frank Wills placed his call to the Metropolitan Police Department Second District at approximately 1:47 AM on June 17, 1972. The call is recorded in both his Security Officer's Log and the Metropolitan Police Department arrest report as the initiating event of the police response.

choice_echoes.source: Washington Metropolitan Police Department arrest report, June 17, 1972; Carl Shoffler testimony, Senate Select Committee on Presidential Campaign Activities, May 18, 1973
choice_echoes.historical_record: Officers Carl Shoffler, John Barrett, and Paul Leeper, riding in unmarked unit 727 assigned to the Tactical Enforcement Branch of the Metropolitan Police Department Second District, were alerted by radio dispatcher at approximately 1:52 AM on June 17, 1972. They arrived at the Watergate office building within a few minutes of the call, working in plainclothes as standard Tactical Enforcement Branch procedure, and arrived without activated lights or siren. A floor-by-floor search of the building followed, resulting in the arrests inside Suite 600.

choice_echoes.source: Alfred Baldwin testimony, Senate Select Committee on Presidential Campaign Activities; Los Angeles Times interview with Baldwin, October 5, 1972
choice_echoes.historical_record: Alfred Baldwin was stationed in Room 723 of the Howard Johnson Motor Lodge on Virginia Avenue NW, directly across from the Watergate complex, serving as lookout and to monitor radio transmissions intercepted from previously planted listening devices.

choice_echoes.source: Washington Metropolitan Police Department arrest inventory, June 17, 1972; Washington Metropolitan Police Department arrest report, June 17, 1972; Senate Select Committee on Presidential Campaign Activities exhibit records
choice_echoes.historical_record: Five men were working inside the Democratic National Committee offices in Suite 600 of the Watergate office building at the time of arrest: Bernard Barker, Virgilio Gonzalez, Eugenio Martinez, James McCord, and Frank Sturgis. Evidence inventoried at arrest included bugging equipment, two 35mm cameras, forty rolls of unexposed film, lock picks, and consecutively serialized cash. A short-wave radio receiver tuned to the Metropolitan Police Department's dispatch frequency was also recovered and inventoried as part of the team's secondary warning system.

character_fates.name: Alfred Baldwin

primary_source.citation: Alfred Baldwin testimony, Senate Select Committee on Presidential Campaign Activities; Los Angeles Times interview with Baldwin, October 5, 1972

character_fates.historical_record: Alfred Baldwin cooperated with federal investigators and became a key witness for the prosecution. He gave a detailed account of his role as lookout and radio monitor to the Senate Select Committee on Presidential Campaign Activities and provided an extended interview to the Los Angeles Times published on October 5, 1972, which was among the first detailed public accounts of the operation from a participant's perspective. Baldwin pleaded guilty to a reduced charge and received a suspended sentence in exchange for his cooperation. He was not among the men tried in United States v. Liddy et al.

character_fates.name: Bernard Barker

primary_source.citation: Washington Metropolitan Police Department arrest report, June 17, 1972; United States v. Liddy et al., U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia; Washington Metropolitan Police Department arrest inventory, June 17, 1972

character_fates.historical_record: Bernard Barker was arrested inside the Democratic National Committee offices in Suite 600 of the Watergate office building in the early hours of June 17, 1972. He was tried in United States v. Liddy et al. in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia and pleaded guilty. He was sentenced to prison. His personal address book, recovered at arrest, contained the notation 'H.H.' beside a White House telephone number belonging to E. Howard Hunt, a detail that contributed to investigators tracing the operation toward the White House.

character_fates.name: Carl Shoffler

primary_source.citation: Carl Shoffler testimony, Senate Select Committee on Presidential Campaign Activities, May 18, 1973; Washington Metropolitan Police Department arrest report, June 17, 1972

character_fates.historical_record: Carl Shoffler, a plainclothes officer of the Tactical Enforcement Branch of the Metropolitan Police Department Second District, was one of the three officers who responded to Frank Wills's call and conducted the floor-by-floor search that resulted in the arrests inside Suite 600. He testified before the Senate Select Committee on Presidential Campaign Activities on May 18, 1973, providing a detailed account of the response and arrest. He inventoried the evidence recovered at the scene, including the notebook belonging to Eugenio Martinez. Shoffler continued his career with the Metropolitan Police Department.

character_fates.name: Eugenio Martinez

primary_source.citation: Washington Metropolitan Police Department arrest inventory logged by Officer Shoffler, June 17, 1972; United States v. Liddy et al., U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia; Senate Select Committee on Presidential Campaign Activities exhibit records

character_fates.historical_record: Eugenio Martinez was arrested inside the Democratic National Committee offices in Suite 600 of the Watergate office building in the early hours of June 17, 1972. A spiral notebook recovered from him at arrest contained the words 'White House' in his handwriting, and his personal directory contained an entry reading 'W. House.' He was tried in United States v. Liddy et al. and pleaded guilty. He was sentenced to prison. Martinez later gave accounts of his role as a locksmith and CIA operative on the entry team.

character_fates.name: Frank Sturgis

primary_source.citation: Washington Metropolitan Police Department arrest report, June 17, 1972; United States v. Liddy et al., U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia; Senate Select Committee on Presidential Campaign Activities records

character_fates.historical_record: Frank Sturgis was arrested inside the Democratic National Committee offices in Suite 600 of the Watergate office building in the early hours of June 17, 1972. He was tried in United States v. Liddy et al. and pleaded guilty. He was sentenced to prison. His background as a former U.S. military serviceman and anti-Castro operative with connections to CIA-linked Cuban exile groups was established in the trial record and in Senate Select Committee proceedings.

character_fates.name: Frank Wills

primary_source.citation: Frank Wills, Security Officer's Log, Watergate Office Building, June 17, 1972, National Archives, NAID 304970; Washington Metropolitan Police Department arrest report, June 17, 1972

character_fates.historical_record: Frank Wills, employed by General Security Services as a night security guard at the Watergate office building, discovered tape on the garage-level stairwell door latch bolts for the second time at approximately 1:47 AM on June 17, 1972, and placed the call to the Metropolitan Police Department Second District that initiated the response leading to the arrests. His Security Officer's Log for that night is preserved at the National Archives under NAID 304970. Wills received public recognition for his role in initiating the discovery of the break-in, though he did not benefit materially from the notoriety and faced significant financial hardship in subsequent years.

character_fates.name: James McCord

primary_source.citation: United States v. Liddy et al., U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia; Senate Select Committee on Presidential Campaign Activities testimony of James McCord; Washington Metropolitan Police Department arrest report, June 17, 1972

character_fates.historical_record: James McCord was arrested inside the Democratic National Committee offices in Suite 600 of the Watergate office building in the early hours of June 17, 1972. His identity as a former CIA physical security officer and the sitting Security Coordinator for the Committee for the Re-election of the President was established at arrest and became one of the first threads connecting the break-in to the Nixon re-election campaign. He was tried in United States v. Liddy et al. and convicted. Before sentencing, McCord wrote a letter to Judge John Sirica stating that political pressure had been applied to the defendants to plead guilty and remain silent, and that perjury had been committed at trial. This letter, read in open court on March 23, 1973, was a pivotal moment in the unraveling of the cover-up. McCord testified before the Senate Select Committee on Presidential Campaign Activities.

historical_frame.text: The arrests of June 17, 1972 led to United States v. Liddy et al. in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, in which all five men arrested at the Watergate were convicted or pleaded guilty; the trial and its aftermath initiated the chain of congressional and judicial proceedings that became the Watergate scandal.
historical_frame.source: United States v. Liddy et al., U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia; Senate Select Committee on Presidential Campaign Activities final report, 1974

historical_frame.text: The Senate Select Committee on Presidential Campaign Activities, established by Senate Resolution 60 on February 7, 1973, conducted public hearings beginning May 17, 1973, at which participants including McCord, Baldwin, and Shoffler testified under oath about the events of June 17, 1972 and the broader campaign of political espionage and sabotage.
historical_frame.source: Senate Select Committee on Presidential Campaign Activities final report, 1974; Carl Shoffler testimony, Senate Select Committee on Presidential Campaign Activities, May 18, 1973

historical_frame.text: James McCord's letter to Judge John Sirica, read in open court on March 23, 1973, stated that political pressure had been applied to the Watergate defendants to plead guilty and remain silent and that perjury had been committed at trial; the letter is identified in the historical record as a pivotal moment in the collapse of the cover-up that followed the June 17, 1972 arrests.
historical_frame.source: Senate Select Committee on Presidential Campaign Activities final report, 1974; 'Watergate Revisited,' The Washington Post, June 14, 1992

immediate_outcome.summary: Five men — Bernard Barker, Virgilio Gonzalez, Eugenio Martinez, James McCord, and Frank Sturgis — were arrested inside the Democratic National Committee offices in Suite 600 of the Watergate office building in the early hours of June 17, 1972, following a floor-by-floor search by plainclothes Metropolitan Police Department officers responding to Frank Wills's call. Evidence recovered at the scene included bugging equipment, cameras, film, consecutively serialized cash, lock picks, and personal materials linking the arrested men to the White House and to the Committee for the Re-election of the President.

glossary.definition: 1972, when Richard Nixon was seeking re-election against Democrat George McGovern and held a commanding polling lead that made his victory appear certain.
The Watergate building's security guard working the night shift, whose eighty-dollar-a-week salary and job security hinge on his discretion in handling what might be a routine custodian's mistake.
A fixed light fixture mounted above the lobby reception desk that provides the only interior illumination of the Watergate office building's ground floor after hours.
The spring-loaded bolt that extends from a door lock into the strike plate—without it engaging, a door can be opened from the inside at any time.
The metal plate on a doorframe that the latch bolt slides into when a door closes—taping over it prevents the bolt from catching and locking the door.
Adhesive tape used to keep stairwell door latches open so the team can move freely through the building without triggering alarms—discovered by the security guard on multiple rounds.
The specific Howard Johnson hotel room where a lookout has spent eight or nine consecutive nights monitoring audio feeds and watching for security problems across the street.
The hotel across Virginia Avenue from the Watergate office building, where operatives monitored the listening device from an upper-floor room and coordinated the break-in.
A listening device planted in the DNC office in May that had been broadcasting audio to monitors across the street—the 'technical correction' that brings the team back inside on this night.
The administrative headquarters and nerve center of the Democratic Party, occupying the sixth floor of the Watergate complex where campaign strategy, voter files, and internal documents were stored.
New legislation effective April 7, 1972, that required campaigns to report donations publicly—which is why the Committee moved money through intermediary accounts before the deadline.

glossary.term: Committee for the Re-election of the President
glossary.definition: Nixon's official campaign organization in 1972, which raised unprecedented amounts of cash and coordinated financial transfers through Mexico and Miami to avoid the new campaign finance disclosure requirements.

A mixed-use development of office and residential buildings on Virginia Avenue near the Kennedy Center, opened in 1965 on the Potomac's east bank—known simply by its address rather than a proper name.

scenario.description: Washington, D.C., June 17, 1972, twelve minutes before two in the morning. A night guard has found the same tape twice. Five men are working on the sixth floor of the Watergate office building, and the lookout across Virginia Avenue is watching a street that tells him nothing. The macro-outcome is fixed. The ninety minutes before it are yours.

sections.text: It is the summer of a presidential election year, and Richard Nixon leads George McGovern by margins that make the outcome look settled. The Committee for the Re-election of the President has raised more money than any campaign in American history, some of it in cash, some of it moved through accounts in Mexico and Miami before the new campaign finance disclosure law takes effect on April 7. The Democratic National Committee occupies the sixth floor of a glass-and-concrete complex on Virginia Avenue, a building whose name is simply its address — the Watergate — a residential and office development opened in 1965 on the Potomac's east bank, a short walk from the Kennedy Center. Washington in June 1972 is a city that believes it has seen everything, and it has not.

For the five men on the sixth floor, tonight is a technical correction — a transmitter that has been feeding poor audio since May needs to be replaced, and internal campaign documents need to be photographed before the building opens Monday morning. For the man across the street in Room 723, it is the eighth or ninth consecutive night of nothing, and nothing is what he expects. For Frank Wills, what is at stake is narrower and more immediate: eighty dollars a week, a job he cannot afford to lose, and the specific social cost of calling the police over what is probably a custodian's oversight. Nobody in this building, and nobody across the street, understands that the night's outcome will be read in every subsequent decade of American political life.

Virginia Avenue is empty at this hour, the pavement holding the day's heat in a way that makes the air feel used. The Watergate office building's lobby is dark behind its glass facade, the only interior light a security lamp above the reception desk. Across six lanes of asphalt, the Howard Johnson Motor Lodge shows a few lit windows on the upper floors, the television glow of insomnia or a late shift. The Potomac is two blocks west and the night smells of river mud and car exhaust and the particular staleness of a city that has been awake too long. Inside the building, the air conditioning runs at a level calibrated for a full office day, which means it is too cold for one man walking a circuit with a flashlight.

You are at the threshold of ninety minutes that will not feel like history because they do not feel like anything yet — they feel like a shift, a round, a job, a decision about whether to pick up a phone. The tape is there again. The stairwell smells of concrete and motor oil. The flashlight beam catches the adhesive edge, and you are the only person in the building who knows it.

winConditions: As Wills: log the second tape discovery, reach the security phone, and complete the call to the Second District before the round expires.

As McCord: finish replacing the transmitter and clear the team's most compromising pocket litter before the stairwell door opens — the hard floor items cannot be removed, but exposure above the floor can be minimized.
As Baldwin: transmit a warning early enough that McCord receives it on the walkie-talkie before the officers reach the sixth floor.
failConditions: As Wills: second tape is not reported before 2:00 AM, allowing the team additional time to sanitize the suite.
As McCord: transmitter housing is left open and the Miami crew's documents are still spread on the desk when the door opens.
As Baldwin: warning goes out after officers are already on the sixth floor, giving McCord no actionable lead time.

facts.content: Bernard Barker was born in Havana in 1917 to an American father and held United States citizenship. He served in the United States Army Air Forces as a bombardier in the Second World War, was shot down over Germany, and was held as a prisoner of war. He later served in the Cuban police and worked for the CIA, including on operations connected to the Bay of Pigs. He led the Miami-based entry team members participating in the Watergate operation.

facts.content: Frank Wills did not testify before the Senate Select Committee (Ervin Committee); no committee finding concerning his account exists. His actions are documented in his Security Officer's Log (National Archives, NAID 304970) and the Metropolitan Police Department arrest report.

partialSuccessExamples: Wills makes the call but cannot locate a supervisor to log the irregularity, leaving the chain of custody incomplete.
McCord secures the transmitter housing but cannot recover the spiral notebook from Martinez's jacket before the door opens.
Baldwin transmits in time for McCord to hear the warning but not in time for the team to reach the stairwell — five men are still taken, but with fewer documents spread on the desk.
